reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / Oxford Handbook of Endocrinology and Diabetes
clinicalPearls: 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency is a rare autosomal recessive form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia caused by loss-of-function variants in CYP17A1
The enzyme is required for both cortisol synthesis and, through its 17,20-lyase activity, for adrenal and gonadal sex-steroid synthesis, so both cortisol and sex steroids are deficient

Steroid production is shunted into the mineralocorticoid pathway, with accumulation of 11-deoxycorticosterone and corticosterone producing low-renin hypertension with hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis
Cortisol is low but overt adrenal crisis is uncommon because corticosterone provides some glucocorticoid activity

Sex-steroid deficiency causes absent or delayed puberty; genetic females present with primary amenorrhoea and lack of secondary sexual characteristics, and genetic males (46,XY) typically have undervirilised or female-appearing external genitalia
Diagnosis rests on the combination of hypertension with hypokalaemia, low sex steroids and cortisol, raised mineralocorticoid precursors, and elevated gonadotrophins
Management combines glucocorticoid replacement to suppress the mineralocorticoid excess and control hypertension with appropriate sex-hormone replacement at puberty
reference.pathophysiology: 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency results from autosomal recessive variants in CYP17A1, whose enzyme carries out two activities: 17-alpha-hydroxylation, needed for cortisol synthesis, and 17,20-lyase activity, needed to generate androgen and oestrogen precursors in the adrenal and gonad. Loss of both activities lowers cortisol and sex steroids, and the reduced cortisol removes negative feedback so ACTH rises and drives steroidogenesis into the intact mineralocorticoid pathway. Accumulation of 11-deoxycorticosterone and corticosterone, both with mineralocorticoid activity, causes sodium retention, volume expansion and low-renin hypertension with hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, while the raised corticosterone provides enough glucocorticoid effect to usually prevent adrenal crisis. Sex-steroid deficiency impairs sexual development, producing hypogonadism with absent puberty and, in 46,XY individuals, undervirilised or female-appearing genitalia because androgen synthesis fails.
additionalDifferentials: Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (primary amenorrhoea in 46,XY)
Gonadal dysgenesis and other disorders of sex development
additionalInvestigations: Adrenal steroid profile showing raised 11-deoxycorticosterone and corticosterone with low cortisol and sex steroids
Plasma renin and aldosterone (both typically suppressed)
Serum electrolytes for hypokalaemic alkalosis and blood pressure assessment
Karyotype and pelvic/gonadal imaging to clarify sexual development
redFlags: Severe hypertension with hypokalaemia in a young person
Primary amenorrhoea and absent puberty prompting evaluation
Undervirilised genitalia in a 46,XY individual requiring multidisciplinary care
Intra-abdominal gonads with potential malignancy risk
reference.prognosis: With glucocorticoid therapy to reverse the mineralocorticoid excess and control blood pressure and potassium, plus sex-hormone replacement to induce and maintain secondary sexual characteristics, patients can do well; fertility is impaired and long-term outcome depends on blood-pressure control and adherence.
pitfalls: Missing the diagnosis in a phenotypic female presenting with hypertension and delayed puberty
Attributing the hypertension to primary hyperaldosteronism despite suppressed aldosterone
Overlooking the need for sex-hormone replacement at the expected age of puberty
Failing to identify and manage intra-abdominal gonads in 46,XY individuals
Over- or under-replacing glucocorticoid when balancing blood-pressure control against iatrogenic effects
references: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline on congenital adrenal hyperplasia
